quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the OS's definitional lenses covered in this course?
quiz.explanation: Web Browser isn't a way of defining an OS at all — it's an application that RUNS on one. The real lenses are Process Manager, Memory Manager, Interface, File/Storage Manager, Resource Manager, and Control Program/Extended Machine.

quiz.question: Jobs are grouped and run back-to-back with zero human interaction until the whole group finishes. This describes:
quiz.explanation: Batch OS — the defining trait is no interaction mid-run, and an individual job has to wait for the entire batch ahead of it to clear, laundry-day style.

quiz.question: An OS accepting new hardware, features, and security patches without needing a full rebuild each time reflects which OS objective?
quiz.explanation: Ability to evolve — one of the three core objectives (alongside Convenience and Efficiency), and exactly why your phone survives an OS update instead of needing replacement.

quiz.question: True or False: Dispatching and quantum both refer to the exact same underlying concept.
quiz.explanation: False — dispatching is the EVENT of handing the CPU to a process; quantum is the DURATION that process is then allowed to keep it. One starts the turn, the other limits it.

quiz.question: A process has a burst time of 18ms on a system using a 6ms quantum (time slice). How many full rounds of CPU time does it need to finish?
quiz.explanation: 3 rounds — 18ms of total work divided into 6ms slices means the process gets dispatched, runs out its quantum, and gets re-queued three separate times before it's actually done.

quiz.question: What specific limitation of batch processing directly forced the shift to multiprogramming?
options: Batch systems couldn't store results on disk
The CPU sat idle every time a job was waiting on I/O, wasting expensive hardware
Batch systems had no Job Control Language
Users weren't allowed to submit more than one job
quiz.explanation: The CPU idling during I/O waits is exactly what multiprogramming fixed — keeping several jobs in memory so the CPU could switch to another one instead of sitting idle.

quiz.question: A user explicitly knows they're pulling a file from "the shared drive on Server B" in their office. This is best described as a:
quiz.explanation: Network OS — the defining test is whether the user knows/cares which machine they're on. In a Distributed OS, that same request would be invisibly routed with the user none the wiser.

quiz.question: Which RTOS characteristic means a task takes exactly the same amount of time to complete every single time it runs?
quiz.explanation: Deterministic — the defining RTOS trait. Priority-based scheduling and fault tolerance are also RTOS characteristics, but they describe different things (who runs next, and how failures are handled).

theory.question: State at least five distinct definitional lenses for an operating system, briefly explaining each.
theory.modelAnswer: An operating system can be defined through at least six lenses. As a Process Manager, it creates, schedules, and terminates processes, giving each a fair share of CPU time. As a Memory Manager, it decides how RAM is allocated across running programs and reclaims memory that's no longer needed. As an Interface, it provides the layer (windows, icons, command line) through which users interact with the machine without touching hardware directly. As a File/Storage Manager, it organises raw disk space into a navigable structure of files and folders. As a Resource Manager, it allocates CPU, memory, and I/O devices fairly across competing programs. And as a Control Program / Extended Machine, it simultaneously polices programs to prevent them from misbehaving or interfering with each other, while abstracting away hardware complexity so users never need to think in binary. Each lens describes the same OS from a different angle, and a question asking for a definition 'in terms of' a specific area expects the answer to come from that specific lens.
keyPoints: Process Manager — creates, schedules, terminates processes
Memory Manager — allocates and reclaims RAM
Interface — the layer between user and hardware
File/Storage Manager — organises disk space into files/folders
Resource Manager — allocates CPU, memory, I/O fairly
Control Program / Extended Machine — prevents misuse, abstracts hardware

theory.question: Differentiate between Batch OS, Time-Sharing OS, and Distributed OS, and explain the specific limitation of each earlier era that forced the emergence of the next.
theory.modelAnswer: Batch OS groups similar jobs together and runs them back-to-back with no human interaction during execution — efficient for hardware utilisation overall, but an individual job has to wait for the entire batch ahead of it to finish, sometimes for hours. Time-Sharing OS lets multiple human users interact with one machine simultaneously, each receiving a small rotating slice of CPU time fast enough to feel like uninterrupted personal access. Distributed OS coordinates many physically separate machines so seamlessly that they present the illusion of being a single system, with the user never knowing or caring which actual machine handled their request. In terms of evolution, batch processing emerged because the earlier one-job-at-a-time era wasted expensive hardware on idle waiting between manually-loaded jobs. Batch processing itself was limited because the CPU still sat idle whenever a job was waiting on I/O, and users had no way to interact with a running job — this forced multiprogramming (switching to another job during I/O waits) and then time-sharing (giving live human users rotating access). Time-sharing was still limited to one physical machine's capacity, which eventually forced the move to distributed systems, spreading work across many machines to overcome the ceiling any single machine would eventually hit.
keyPoints: Batch — jobs queued, no interaction, whole batch must finish
Time-Sharing — multiple users, rotating CPU slices, feels simultaneous
Distributed — many machines, one illusion of a single system
Batch emerged to fix wasted idle hardware from one-job-at-a-time computing
Multiprogramming/time-sharing emerged to fix batch's CPU idling and lack of interactivity
Distributed systems emerged to overcome a single machine's scaling ceiling
